description: My background is in psychology, wellbeing, and psychotherapy, with experience in designing and delivering digital mental health programmes, from CBT and ACT-based content to user engagement. I’m UX-trained and now studying Human Centred AI, bringing user insight, behaviour-change design, and project delivery to products that help people.
summary:
Orbit Baseline is an interactive prototype of a personal self-care and early intervention support tool for astronauts on long missions. It is trainable by the astronaunt and ground team over time, and It gathers health indicators with wearable technology and self-reporting (sleep, heart rate variability, skin conductance, breathing, temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar, hydration, and mood) and compares each against the astronaut’s own baseline, learned on Earth and adapted for space, rather than a generic range; it orbits personal baselines. It also uses a psychological 360 view that weighs how the person says they feel, treating a gap between the data and the person’s report as useful information, while being observed by experts back at base. 

When early drift (from individual baseline norm) appears, the app offers personalised, doable actions, from breathing and body-based practices to rest, play, or an immersive sensory space with VR, and learns from 'Was this helpful?' feedback. A blended-care model keeps flight surgeons and psychotherapists in the loop, with the astronaut choosing what to share, which suits deep-space communication delays. Supported with a COM-B design for digital mental health.

It matters because on missions far from Earth, astronauts must notice problems in themselves early and act. Orbit Baseline supports care before crisis. The prototype uses simulated data. In operation, it draws data from wearable technology and user self-reporting.
details:
Orbit Baseline is a dashboard-style monitoring app that helps astronauts understand their body and mind over time, learns each person’s patterns to guide personalised training and therapeutic support within a blended-care model, and is designed to link with and create VR experiences tailored to their needs.

What it does and how it works
Orbit Baseline is an interactive web prototype, built with AI support, that monitors nine indicators: sleep, heart rate variability, skin conductance, breathing, temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar, hydration and mood (which includes energy levels and cognitive executive functioning). Each is read against the astronaut’s own baseline, not a population range. The baseline is learned on Earth and can be switched to a space baseline to allow for expected changes such as fluid shifts and disturbed sleep.

A gauge, a body map, and a trends view show progress daily across a mission. If a signal stays outside the person’s range for three days, the app suggests an addtional matched action, such as breathing, a body scan, rest, movement, play, a message from home or an immersive sensory space, and explains why.

Mind and body prompts (Was this helpful?, body-map sensations and personal notes) are compared with the data. Any gap is treated as useful information, and the answers are used to adjust the astronaut’s baseline over time.

Benefits and intended impact
Problems are noticed early, so support comes before crisis. Self-care becomes practical for people far from help and facing long communication delays. In a blended-care model, the astronaut chooses what to share with flight surgeons and psychotherapists, who can review trends and adjust the plan.

What makes it creative
It links data to the felt body (somatic) through a tappable body map and sensation words. It treats the astronaut’s own report as equal to the sensors. It shows wellbeing as a spectrum of greens rather than simply red, amber or green alerts, and it personalises support, with immersive VR spaces as a future concept. It places emphasis on body and mind connection.

Tools used
The prototype is a single HTML, CSS and JavaScript page with simulated data and no hardware. I designed the concept, clinical logic and care model from my background as a psychotherapist and somatic wellbeing practitioner. I used Claude (an AI assistant) to help build the prototype and draft text, and Canva for mock-ups and slides. A screen recording shows the app in use.

Factors considered
Individual differences in physiology, difficulty noticing or reporting body signals (interoception issues), privacy and consent, and the risk of over-monitoring. The design considered the five NASA hazards, especially isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, and a closed environment. Thresholds and space adjustments are illustrative and would need clinical and flight-medicine validation. It is trained by individuals over time so is longitudinal design.
